The tribunal of the Holy Office set up in Mexico City in 1571 to police faith and morals in New Spain, a branch of the Spanish Inquisition. It was abolished in 1820, just before Mexican independence.

Before 1571, friars and bishops had run trials themselves, sometimes against Indigenous people. One such case, the burning of a Nahua lord of Texcoco in 1539, caused alarm in Spain. When the formal tribunal came, Indigenous people were placed outside its reach, as new converts, and left to the bishops.

Its targets were Spaniards, people of mixed descent and Africans:

  • converted Jews accused of secretly keeping Judaism, the main victims of its harshest trials in the 1590s and 1640s
  • Protestants, often foreign sailors and pirates
  • bigamy, blasphemy, witchcraft and banned books

It held public autos de fe, though far fewer people were executed than in Spain. In its last years it tried independence leaders, among them the priest Miguel Hidalgo.
sum: The tribunal of the Holy Office set up in Mexico City in 1571 to police faith and morals in New Spain, a branch of the Spanish Inquisition. It was abolished in 1820, just before Mexican independence.
